Man
MAN
n. (the human creature made in God's image; also, specifically, the male of the species; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'adam, 'īsh, 'enōsh, geber and Greek anthrōpos, anēr)
From Old English mann, common Germanic, originally meaning “human being” without regard to sex; the sex-specific sense (over against wifman, whence woman) grew alongside it and both senses are alive in the Authorized Version. Hebrew 'adam carries the same double duty and is bound by a pun to 'adamah, the ground: the man is the earthling, formed of dust. 'īsh is the male over against 'ishshah, the woman taken out of him (Gen 2:23). Greek anthrōpos is the human being; anēr is the man as male and husband.

Biblical Definition

Man is the creature God made last on the sixth day, male and female, in His own image and after His likeness, to have dominion over the works of His hands. He is dust and breath together: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). He is therefore neither a beast nor an angel but a body-soul unity, mortal in his frame and immortal in his soul, made for worship and for work. The image is not a faculty man possesses but a status he bears, and it is not forfeited by the Fall: after Eden, murder is still capital because the image is still there (Gen 9:6). Yet the whole man fell in Adam — mind, will, affections, body — so that by nature he is dead in trespasses and sins and cannot of himself turn to God. Scripture answers this ruin not with a program of improvement but with a second Man: “The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” (1Co 15:47). The Psalmist's astonishment — “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” (Psa 8:4) — is answered finally in the Incarnation, where God took this nature to Himself and did not lay it down.

Webster 1828 Definition

The human creature, male and female, made in the image of God, formed of the dust and animated by the breath of God; a body-soul unity, fallen in Adam, redeemable only in Christ the second Man.

MAN, n. plu. men. [Sax. man, mann; Goth. manna.] 1. Mankind; the human race; the whole species of human beings. And God said, Let us make man in our image. Gen. 1.

2. A male individual of the human race, of adult growth or years. And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman. Gen. 2.

3. A servant, an attendant, a dependent; one under the authority or in the household of another.

4. Man is used to denote the human nature considered in its weakness and mortality, over against God: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in man.” Ps. 118. This is the sense of Isaiah's “Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils.”

5. In theology, the old man and the new man (Rom 6:6; Eph 4:22–24; Col 3:9–10) name not two persons but the whole man as he stands in Adam and as he stands in Christ — the corrupted nature to be put off and the renewed nature to be put on.

Key Scripture

Gen 1:27 — "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."

Gen 2:7 — "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

Psa 8:4 — "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?"

1Co 15:47 — "The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven."

Modern Corruption

Two corruptions run in opposite directions and meet in the same place: naturalism, which makes man an accident of matter with no image to bear, and gender ideology, which detaches the person from the embodied sex God gave him — both denying that Gen 1:27 is a statement about what a human being actually is.

expand to see more

Philosophical naturalism defines man as a complicated animal, the product of undirected process, whose sense of dignity is an evolutionary artifact. Everything the Bible calls man — image-bearer, worshipper, covenant party, moral agent answerable at a judgment — is on that account a useful fiction. The corruption is rarely announced; it arrives as an assumption in a textbook, and its pastoral fruit is despair, because a creature with no Maker has no ground for the worth he cannot stop believing he has. Scripture's answer is not that man is grander than he thought but that he is dustier and more honored at once: formed of the ground, and crowned with glory and honour (Psa 8:5).

The second corruption grants that man is more than matter and then severs him from his body. Modern gender identity theory holds that the inward sense of self is the real person and the sexed body a contingent circumstance to be brought into line with it. Gen 1:27 forecloses this: God created them male and female, and the Lord Jesus grounded the whole doctrine of marriage on that clause (Mat 19:4). Sex is creational, embodied, and given — not assigned, not chosen, and not a costume. The church owes every person caught in this confusion the full dignity of the image he bears and the full truth about the body he was given; the one without the other is not compassion but abandonment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'adam (humankind, bound by pun to 'adamah, ground), 'īsh (male, husband), 'enōsh (man in his frailty), geber (the strong man); Greek anthrōpos (human being) and anēr (male, husband).

expand to see more

'adam (Hebrew, H120) — humankind generically and the first man personally; the wordplay with 'adamah (ground, H127) is the point of Gen 2:7 and of the sentence “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.”

'īsh (Hebrew, H376) — the male, and by extension the husband; paired with 'ishshah (woman, H802) in Gen 2:23, where the naming establishes the creational order Paul reasons from in 1Co 11:8–9.

'enōsh (Hebrew, H582) — man in his weakness and mortality; the word in Psa 8:4a, which is why the verse is a confession of frailty before it is a celebration of dignity.

anthrōpos (Greek, G444) — human being; the New Testament's word in the Adam-Christ parallels (Rom 5:12–19; 1Co 15:21–22, 45–49), where the whole argument depends on Adam being a historical man and not a symbol.

1689 London Baptist Confession 4.2 and 6.1–3 — man created upright with the law written on his heart, and the whole race falling in Adam as the covenant head, so that original sin is imputed and corruption inherited.

Usage

"The Authorized Version's generic man is not a slip to be edited out. It renders a Hebrew and Greek usage in which the male name stands for the race — a linguistic pattern that carries the doctrine of headship, and which Rom 5:12 requires in order to argue at all."

"“What is man?” is asked three times in Scripture (Job 7:17; Psa 8:4; Psa 144:3) and answered differently each time — a creature too small to be worth God's notice, and yet noticed; the tension resolves only at Bethlehem."

"Preachers should mark that Paul calls Christ the second man, not the third or the millionth: in redemptive history there are exactly two men whose acts count for others, and every human being stands under one or the other."
